title: Zehō
translation: The priest Zehō knew his Pure Land teaching as well as anyone, but he never set himself up as a scholar. He just called on the Buddha's name from morning till night and lived his life in peace. That's the way to do it.
original: {是法法師|ぜほふほふし}は、{浄土宗|じやうどしゆう}に{恥|は}ぢずと{雖|いへど}も、{学匠|がくしやう}をたてず、ただ{明暮|あけくれ}{念仏|ねんぶつ}して、やすらかに{世|よ}を{過|すぐ}すありさま、いとあらまほし。
literal: The priest Zehō, although he was not put to shame in the Pure Land school, did not set himself up as a scholar, but only recited the nenbutsu morning and evening and passed through the world peacefully: this way of being is very desirable.

notes.text: Zehō is probably a contemporary of Kenkō. Little else about him is certain.
The Pure Land school, founded by Hōnen (1133–1212). Its teaching is that you are saved by calling on Amida Buddha, by reciting {南無阿弥陀仏|なむあみだぶつ}. That recitation is the {念仏|ねんぶつ} of this section.

{恥|は}ぢず: 'not put to shame', so 'not inferior to anyone'. He knew the teaching well enough to stand next to anyone in his school. と{雖|いへど}も: 'although', a phrase from reading Chinese texts aloud in Japanese.
{学匠|がくしやう}: a scholar-monk. たてず: 'did not set up, did not claim'. He had the learning and did not make it his position.
{明暮|あけくれ}: 'dawn and dusk', so 'all day, all the time'.
あらまほし: 'ideal, what one would wish for', the word Kenkō uses in section 1 for the hermit who has really walked away from it all.
